st: Cut the cabbage into quarters through the core, then cut into 2-inch pieces.
Dissolve [[0.33 cup]] salt in [[4 cups]] water, pour over the cabbage, and let sit for 1.5 hours, turning once.
Rinse the cabbage 3 times in cold water, then drain well for 20 minutes.
Stir [[1 tbsp]] rice flour into [[0.5 cup]] water in a small pot and cook over medium heat for 2 minutes until thick. Cool completely.
Mix the paste with [[0.33 cup]] chili flakes, [[6 cloves]] garlic, [[1 tbsp]] ginger, [[3 tbsp]] fish sauce and [[1 tsp]] sugar.
Wearing gloves, toss the radish and scallions with the paste, then add the cabbage and massage until every piece is coated.
Pack tightly into a clean jar, pressing out air pockets, leaving 1 inch at the top.
Leave at room temperature for 1 to 2 days until it smells pleasantly sour, then refrigerate. It keeps for weeks.
Mix the beef with [[2 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tsp]] sugar, [[2 cloves]] garlic and [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil. Let it marinate for 15 minutes.
Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 30 seconds, rinse in cold water, squeeze dry, and toss with [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil and [[1 clove]] garlic.
Boil the bean sprouts for 3 minutes, drain, and toss with [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil, [[1 clove]] garlic and [[0.5 tsp]] salt.
Saute the carrots in [[1 tbsp]] vegetable oil with [[0.5 tsp]] salt for 2 minutes until just tender.
Cook the beef in a hot skillet for 3 minutes until browned and cooked through.
Stir [[4 tbsp]] gochujang with [[1 tsp]] sugar and [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil to make the sauce.
Fry the eggs sunny-side up in [[1 tbsp]] oil until the whites are set.
Divide the rice among 4 bowls. Arrange the beef and vegetables in sections on top and add an egg.
Sprinkle with sesame seeds, add a spoonful of sauce, and mix everything together before eating.
Freeze the beef for 20 minutes to make slicing easier, then slice it very thin against the grain.
Whisk [[0.33 cup]] soy sauce, [[3 tbsp]] sugar, the grated pear, [[5 cloves]] garlic, [[2 tbsp]] sesame oil and [[0.5 tsp]] pepper.
Toss the beef, onion and half the scallions with the marinade. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 30 minutes.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a large skillet or grill pan over high heat until very hot.
Cook the beef in small batches for 2 to 3 minutes until browned and caramelized at the edges. Do not crowd the pan.
Sprinkle with [[1 tbsp]] sesame seeds and the rest of the scallions.
Serve hot with rice and lettuce leaves.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil in a medium pot over medium heat.
Add the pork and cook for 4 minutes until it starts to brown.
Add the kimchi and onion and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until softened.
Stir in [[1 tbsp]] chili flakes, [[3 cloves]] garlic, [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce and [[1 tsp]] sugar.
Pour in [[3 cups]] water and [[0.25 cup]] kimchi juice, bring to a boil, then lower the heat.
Simmer, partly covered, for 20 minutes until the pork is fully cooked and tender.
Add the tofu and simmer 5 more minutes.
Top with scallions and serve bubbling hot with rice.
If the rice cakes are hard or refrigerated, soak them in warm water for 10 minutes and separate them.
Put [[2.5 cups]] water, [[3 tbsp]] gochujang, [[1 tbsp]] chili flakes, [[2 tbsp]] sugar, [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce and [[2 cloves]] garlic in a wide pan. Stir until mixed.
Bring the sauce to a boil over medium-high heat.
Add the rice cakes and cook for 8 minutes, stirring often so they do not stick.
Add the fish cakes and eggs and cook for 4 minutes until the sauce thickens and clings.
Add the scallions and cook 1 more minute.
Serve hot straight from the pan. The rice cakes should be soft and chewy.
Marinate the beef with [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tsp]] sugar, [[1 clove]] garlic and [[1 tsp]] sesame oil for 10 minutes.
Boil the noodles for 6 minutes until soft and chewy, then drain, rinse in cold water, and cut into shorter lengths with scissors.
Blanch the spinach for 30 seconds, rinse cold, squeeze dry, and toss with [[1 tsp]] soy sauce and [[1 tsp]] sesame oil.
Stir-fry the carrots and onion in [[1 tbsp]] oil over medium-high heat for 3 minutes. Remove to a large bowl.
Cook the beef in [[1 tbsp]] oil for 3 minutes until cooked through and add to the bowl.
Mix [[3 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] sugar, [[2 tbsp]] sesame oil and [[2 cloves]] garlic in a pan, add the noodles, and stir over medium heat for 2 minutes until they take on the color.
Add the noodles to the bowl with the spinach and mix by hand until well combined.
Finish with [[1 tbsp]] sesame seeds and [[0.25 tsp]] pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

ing: red leaf or green leaf, separated
st: Mix [[3 tbsp]] sesame oil with [[1 tsp]] salt and [[0.5 tsp]] pepper in a small dish for dipping.
Pat the pork belly dry. Wash and drain the lettuce.
Heat a large skillet or grill pan over medium-high heat. No oil is needed.
Cook the pork in a single layer for 3 to 4 minutes per side until browned and crisp, reaching at least 145°F (63°C).
Add the sliced garlic and kimchi to the pan fat and cook 3 minutes until golden.
Cut the cooked pork into bite-size pieces with kitchen scissors.
To eat, place a piece of pork on a lettuce leaf, add garlic and [[1 tsp]] ssamjang, wrap, and eat in one bite.
Serve with rice, kimchi and the sesame oil dip.
Pat the chicken very dry and season with [[1 tsp]] salt and [[0.5 tsp]] pepper.
Whisk [[0.5 cup]] flour, [[0.5 cup]] cornstarch and [[0.75 cup]] cold water into a thin batter. Coat the chicken in it.
Heat [[6 cups]] oil in a deep heavy pot to 325°F (165°C).
Fry the chicken in batches for 10 minutes until pale golden. Drain on a rack.
Rest for 10 minutes, then raise the oil to 375°F (190°C).
Fry again for 4 to 5 minutes until deep golden and very crisp. The chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).
Simmer [[3 tbsp]] gochujang, [[3 tbsp]] honey, [[2 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[4 cloves]] garlic, [[1 tbsp]] vinegar and [[1 tbsp]] brown sugar in a pan for 3 minutes until syrupy.
Toss the hot chicken in the glaze, sprinkle with [[1 tbsp]] sesame seeds, and serve at once.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] vegetable oil and [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil in a small pot over medium heat.
Add the pork and cook for 3 minutes until no longer pink.
Stir in [[1.5 tbsp]] chili flakes and [[2 cloves]] garlic and cook for 30 seconds, being careful not to burn the flakes.
Add [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce and [[1.5 cups]] water, bring to a boil.
Add the clams and cook 3 minutes, until they open. Discard any that stay shut.
Spoon in the tofu in large chunks and simmer for 5 minutes. Season with [[0.25 tsp]] salt.
Crack the eggs on top, cover, and cook for 1 minute until the whites start to set.
Sprinkle with scallions and serve boiling hot with rice.
Whisk [[1 cup]] flour, [[0.25 cup]] cornstarch, [[0.5 tsp]] salt and [[1 cup]] cold water into a smooth, thin batter.
Mix [[3 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] vinegar and [[0.5 tsp]] chili flakes for the dipping sauce.
Heat [[2 tbsp]] oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium-high heat.
Lay half the scallions in the pan in a flat layer, pour half the batter over them, and top with half the shrimp and squid.
Pour a beaten egg over the top and cook for 4 minutes until the bottom is crisp and the edges lift.
Flip carefully, press down, and cook 3 more minutes, until the seafood is opaque and cooked through.
Repeat with the remaining ingredients and [[2 tbsp]] oil.
Cut into squares and serve hot with the dipping sauce.
Put [[3 tbsp]] doenjang and [[2 tbsp]] gochujang in a small bowl.
Finely mince [[2 cloves]] garlic and the scallions.
Add the garlic and scallions to the bowl.
Stir in [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil and [[1 tbsp]] honey until smooth.
Loosen with [[1 tbsp]] water if it is too stiff to spread.
Taste and add more honey if too salty or more gochujang if you want heat.
Top with [[1 tsp]] sesame seeds and serve with grilled meat and lettuce.
Stir [[2 tsp]] yeast and [[2 tbsp]] sugar into [[1 cup]] warm milk and wait 5 minutes until foamy.
Mix in [[2.5 cups]] flour, [[0.5 tsp]] salt and [[1 tbsp]] oil to make a sticky dough.
Cover and let rise in a warm place for 1 hour until doubled.
Mix [[0.5 cup]] brown sugar, [[1 tsp]] cinnamon and [[0.25 cup]] peanuts for the filling.
Oil your hands, divide the dough into 8 pieces, and flatten each in your palm.
Place about [[1 tbsp]] filling in the center, pinch the dough closed, and roll into a ball.
Heat [[2 tbsp]] oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat. Place the balls seam side down.
After 1 minute, press each flat with a spatula and cook 2 to 3 minutes per side until golden and the sugar has melted.
Let cool 2 minutes before eating, as the syrup is very hot.

ing: 6 for the muffin tin and 1 for the batter
st: Preheat the oven to 375°F and generously butter 6 wells of a muffin tin.
In a bowl whisk one egg with the milk, sugar, vanilla and [[3 tbsp]] melted butter until smooth.
Sift in the flour, baking powder and salt, and stir gently until just combined with no dry streaks. Do not overmix.
Fill each muffin cup halfway with batter, about 3 tablespoons each.
Crack one whole egg into the middle of each cup, gently pressing the yolk into the batter without breaking it.
Bake 18 to 22 minutes until the batter is golden and the egg white is fully set and the yolk is firm; eggs must reach 160°F. Sprinkle with parsley and serve warm.
nt: Baked at 375°F
Best swap: make it dairy-free with plant milk and oil, same amounts, in place of milk and butter.

st: Soak [[1 cup]] malt powder in [[6 cup]] warm water for 1 hour, then rub it with your hands to release the starch.
Let it settle for 30 minutes, then carefully pour off the clear liquid through a cloth, leaving the sediment behind.
Mix the clear liquid with [[2 cup]] cooked rice in a rice cooker or pot. Keep warm at 140°F to 150°F for 4 to 5 hours until the rice grains float to the top.
Rinse a few rice grains in cold water and set them aside for garnish. Put the sweet liquid in a pot with the ginger and [[0.5 cup]] sugar.
Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then simmer for 10 minutes. Chill completely in the fridge.
Serve cold in bowls with the reserved rice grains and a few pine nuts floating on top.
nt: Rice slowly saccharified with malt at a steady low warmth, then boiled
Best swap: no malt powder, use sprouted barley flour, though the sweetness will be milder.

st: Mix the pork, tofu, kimchi, cabbage, 2 cloves garlic, [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce and the sesame oil thoroughly with your hand.
Put a tablespoon of filling on each wrapper. Wet the edge, fold in half and pleat to seal, then pinch the two ends together into a half moon.
Bring the broth to a boil with the remaining garlic and [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce. Simmer 10 minutes.
Drop in the dumplings and simmer for 8 minutes, until they float and the pork reaches 160°F.
Slowly pour the beaten egg in a thin stream around the pot. Wait 20 seconds before stirring so it forms ribbons, and make sure the egg is fully set.
Season with salt, then ladle into bowls and top with scallions.
nt: Simmered in beef broth
Best swap: use vegetable broth and omit the pork, doubling the tofu, for a vegetarian bowl.

st: Freeze the milk or water in a flat tray until solid. Chill two bowls in the freezer.
Shave or blender-pulse the frozen block into very fine snow.
Warm the tteok in a pan of simmering water for 2 minutes if firm, then drain and cool.
Mound the shaved ice in the bowls and spoon the red bean paste on top.
Add the tteok, drizzle with the condensed milk and dust with the soybean powder.
Garnish with sliced almonds, mix at the table and eat quickly.
nt: Don't cook: shaved ice with toppings
Best swap: use kinako (roasted soy flour) if you cannot find injeolmi powder, or fruit in place of the red beans.

st: Wash the pear, apples, persimmons, grapes and strawberries in cold water. Dry them completely with a clean towel.
Peel the Korean pear and apples, then cut each into eight wedges. Remove the core with a small slanted cut.
Soak the pear and apple wedges in ice water with [[1 tbsp]] lemon juice for 3 minutes. This stops browning, then drain them well.
Peel the persimmons and cut into half-moon slices about 1 cm thick. Pull the mandarins into neat segments and pick off the white strings.
To make apple rabbits, cut a V-notch into the skin on each wedge and peel back to the center, leaving the skin as ears.
Arrange the fruit in a circle on a plate or tray, alternating colors, with the small fruit in the middle.
Serve chilled with forks or picks, ideally within 20 minutes.
nt: Don't cook: cut and arrange
Best swap: Asian pear or a very crisp, juicy Bosc pear for Korean pear, and any firm sweet apple for the persimmons.

st: Soak the ribs in cold water for 30 minutes to draw out blood, then drain and pat dry.
Combine the grated pear, [[0.5 cup]] soy sauce, [[3 tbsp]] brown sugar, garlic, [[2 tbsp]] sesame oil, scallions and pepper.
Pour over the ribs, turn to coat, then cover and marinate in the fridge at least 4 hours, up to overnight.
Heat a grill or cast iron grill pan to high. Shake excess marinade off the ribs so they sear instead of steam.
Grill the ribs 2 to 3 minutes per side until charred and caramelized at the edges and cooked through to 145°F.
Cut the meat off the bones with scissors, sprinkle with [[1 tbsp]] sesame seeds and serve with lettuce, rice and ssamjang.
nt: Grilled over high direct heat, thin cut for fast char
Best swap: broil on a tray 4 inches from the heat, 3 minutes per side. Use grated sweet apple plus 1 tsp lemon juice for Asian pear.

st: Pat the tofu slabs very dry with paper towels and sprinkle lightly with salt. Dry tofu browns instead of steaming.
Heat [[2 tbsp]] neutral oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium-high heat. Fry the tofu until deep golden on each side, about 4 minutes per side.
Mix [[3 tbsp]] soy sauce, the gochugaru, garlic, sugar, [[2 tsp]] sesame oil, half the scallions and [[0.5 cup]] water in a bowl.
Pour the sauce over the tofu in the skillet. Reduce the heat to medium-low, cover and simmer for 6 minutes, spooning sauce over the tofu halfway.
Uncover and cook for 2 minutes until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Top with the remaining scallions and [[1 tsp]] sesame seeds. Serve hot with rice.
nt: Pan-fried, then braised
Best swap: use gochugaru-free chili like cayenne at half the amount, or add 1 tbsp gochujang for deeper heat.

st: Slice the cucumbers into 1/4 inch rounds and toss with [[1 tsp]] salt in a bowl. Rest for 15 minutes.
Squeeze the cucumbers gently in your hands and pour off the water that collects, so the seasoning clings.
Add [[1.5 tbsp]] gochugaru, the minced garlic, green onion, [[1 tbsp]] rice vinegar and [[1 tsp]] sugar.
Toss with clean hands or tongs until every slice is coated in red.
Stir in [[1 tsp]] sesame oil and the sesame seeds. Serve fresh as a side for barbecue, or chill up to a day.
nt: Don't cook: salted and seasoned by hand
Best swap: paprika with a pinch of cayenne in place of gochugaru, same amount.

st: Cook the rice with [[2.25 cups]] water, about 18 minutes. Mix with [[1 tbsp]] sesame oil, the salt and sesame seeds while hot, then cool to warm.
Blanch the spinach for 30 seconds, rinse in cold water, squeeze dry, and toss with a drop of sesame oil and a pinch of salt.
Sauté the carrot in a lightly oiled pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until just tender.
Cook the beaten eggs in a thin sheet in a nonstick pan until fully set, then cut into long strips.
Lay a seaweed sheet shiny side down on a bamboo mat. Spread a thin layer of rice, leaving 1 inch bare at the far edge.
Arrange the fillings in a line near the near edge. Roll tightly using the mat, pressing firmly, and seal with a few grains of rice.
Brush the rolls with the remaining sesame oil and slice with a sharp wet knife into 1 inch pieces.
nt: Rice steamed, vegetables blanched or sautéed, egg pan-cooked
Best swap: add tofu or cooked beef bulgogi in place of egg, 4 oz per roll, for more protein.

ing: flounder or snapper, previously frozen, thin sliced
st: Use only sushi-grade fish that has been frozen, thawed in the refrigerator and kept below 40°F until serving.
Whisk [[3 tbsp]] gochujang, [[1 tbsp]] rice vinegar, [[1 tbsp]] sugar and [[1 tsp]] sesame oil into a smooth sauce.
Slice the cold fish against the grain into thin pieces about 1/8 inch thick.
Divide the warm rice between two bowls. Add the lettuce, cucumber and perilla in neat piles.
Lay the fish on top and drizzle on the remaining sesame oil.
Top with sesame seeds and serve with the sauce on the side. Mix everything together just before eating.
nt: Don't cook: raw fish over rice, sauce whisked cold
Best swap: cooked salmon or smoked trout in place of raw fish, same weight, if raw seafood is a concern.

st: Place the anchovies in a dry wide pan over medium-low heat. Stir for 3 minutes until crisp and fragrant, then tip onto a plate.
Wipe the pan, then add [[1 tbsp]] cooking oil and the garlic. Cook over low heat for 30 seconds until fragrant but not brown.
Add [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] sugar and [[2 tbsp]] corn syrup. Simmer 2 minutes until bubbly and slightly thick.
Return the anchovies to the pan and toss quickly for 1 minute so every piece is glazed. Turn off the heat.
Stir in [[1 tsp]] sesame oil and [[1 tbsp]] sesame seeds. Spread on parchment to cool so the pieces do not clump.
Cool fully, then pack into a lunchbox next to rice and kimchi. It keeps a week in the fridge.
nt: Dry pan-toasted, then glazed
Best swap: honey for corn syrup 1:1; add 1 sliced fresh chili in the garlic step for a spicy version.

st: Put the beef, water and [[2 clove]] of the garlic in a pot. Bring to a boil, then skim off the foam and lower the heat. Simmer for 45 minutes until the beef is tender.
Lift out the beef and tear it into thin shreds. Toss with the sesame oil, a pinch of pepper and half the scallions. Keep the broth hot.
Season the broth with the soy sauce, salt and the rest of the garlic. Drain the soaked rice cakes and add them. Simmer 6 to 8 minutes until they float and feel soft and chewy.
While they cook, beat the egg whites and yolks separately. Pan fry each in a lightly oiled nonstick pan over low heat as a thin sheet for 1 to 2 minutes until fully set. Cut into thin strips.
Ladle the soup into bowls. Top with the shredded beef, egg strips, remaining scallions and crumbled seaweed. Serve at once, before the rice cakes get gummy.
nt: Simmered beef broth, with fried egg garnish
Best swap: use 8 cups of shiitake and kombu stock in place of beef broth for a vegetarian soup.

st: Heat the oil [[0.25 cup]] in a wok or deep skillet over medium heat. Add the black bean paste and fry for 3 minutes, stirring, to cook out the bitterness. Scrape it into a bowl.
In the same pan over medium-high heat, cook the pork for 5 minutes until browned. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds.
Add the onion, potato and zucchini. Stir-fry for 6 minutes until the onions turn translucent.
Return the fried paste to the pan with the sugar and [[1.5 cup]] water. Bring to a simmer and cook 10 minutes until the potato is tender.
Stir the starch slurry and pour it in while stirring. Simmer for 1 minute until the sauce is glossy and thick.
Boil the noodles as the package directs, usually 4 to 6 minutes. Drain and rinse briefly in hot water.
Divide the noodles among bowls, ladle the sauce over the top and finish with the cucumber matchsticks.
nt: Paste fried in oil, stir-fried, then simmered
Best swap: if you cannot find chunjang, use Chinese sweet bean sauce and a little extra sugar; swap pork for diced shiitake and tofu for a vegetarian version.

ing: mu, peeled and cut into 1 inch cubes
st: Toss the radish cubes with [[1 tbsp]] salt and let them sit for 1 hour until they release liquid and turn slightly translucent.
Dissolve [[2 tbsp]] salt and [[1 tbsp]] sugar in [[6 cups]] filtered water to make the brine. Taste it; it should be pleasantly salty.
Place the pear, garlic, ginger and scallions in a cloth bag or tie them loosely in a square of cheesecloth so the brine stays clear.
Pack the radish and the bundle in a clean glass jar. Pour the brine over so everything is fully submerged, leaving 1 inch of headspace.
Leave at room temperature for 1 to 2 days, until small bubbles appear and the brine tastes tangy. Open the lid briefly each day to release gas.
Move the jar to the refrigerator for at least 2 more days. Serve very cold in small bowls, with brine, alongside noodles or rice cakes.
nt: Salted and lacto-fermented, don't cook; ferments 1 to 2 days warm, then 2 or more days cold
Best swap: ripe Bosc pear for Asian pear, and daikon for Korean radish at the same weight.

st: Soak the mackerel chunks in cold water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat dry.
Mix the gochugaru, soy sauce, gochujang, garlic, ginger, sugar and rice wine with [[0.5 cup]] water into a sauce.
Spread the radish slices over the base of a wide pot and pour in [[1 cup]] water. Boil for 8 minutes until slightly soft.
Lay the fish on the radish and spoon the sauce on top. Bring to a boil over high heat.
Lower to medium and cook uncovered for 18 minutes, basting the fish every few minutes, until the sauce is thick and the fish is at least 145°F.
Add the scallions and chili and cook 2 more minutes. Serve with rice.
nt: Poached in a spicy braise, basted until glazed
Best swap: canned mackerel or fresh saury; use 1 tbsp more gochujang if you lack gochugaru.

st: Heat the vegetable oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the potatoes cut side down and brown 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds.
Pour in [[1 cup]] water, the soy sauce and sugar. Bring to a boil.
Reduce to medium, cover partly, and simmer 12 minutes until the potatoes are nearly tender.
Add the corn syrup and cook uncovered 6 to 8 minutes, shaking the pan, until the sauce is thick and coats the potatoes.
Turn off the heat, stir in the sesame oil and seeds, and serve warm or at room temperature.
nt: Pan-browned, then braised
Best swap: use honey in place of the corn syrup at the same amount, or maple syrup.
